segments.english: And the LORD went away when he had finished speaking to Abraham, and Abraham returned to his place.
segments.literal: and-went the-LORD as-which finished to-speak to-Abraham and-Abraham returned to-his-place

tokens.note: wayyiqtol of הָלַךְ, 'go' (BDB Qal I.1, of persons); here 'went away', since the speaking has ended.
YHWH, rendered LORD in capitals (decisions: divine names).
kaf of comparison with the relative asher: a temporal conjunction.
piel qatal of kalah, subject the LORD.
piel infinitive construct of dabar with the prefix lamed: 'to speak'.
the vav opens a disjunctive clause; the subject comes first, then the verb.
qal qatal of shuv, 'return, go back'.
lamed with the construct of makom and the 3ms suffix.

phrases.literal: 'and-went the-LORD': the verb comes first in the Hebrew; the English puts the subject first.

phrases.english: when he had finished speaking to Abraham
phrases.literal: 'as-which finished to-speak to-Abraham': the temporal clause, with the subject 'he' understood from the verb.

phrases.english: and Abraham returned to his place
phrases.literal: 'and-Abraham returned to-his-place': the main clause of the second half of the verse.

grammar: The first verb is wayyiqtol (the sequential narrative form, 'and went'); the second half of the verse changes to a disjunctive clause, 'and Abraham returned', with the subject first.
The clause 'when he had finished speaking' is circumstantial: kaf and asher make a temporal conjunction, and the piel qatal kilah gives the completed action before the departure.
The etnahta on Abraham (18:33.7) divides the verse: the first part is the LORD's departure, the second Abraham's return to his place.
The place to which Abraham returns is not named; the commentators identify it (Ibn Ezra: Hebron). See the commentary.
segments.note: The sense is Qal I.1 'go' (of persons); 'went away' adds only the departure that the context gives. The vision-reading of Radak is in the apparatus.

commentary.summary: Rashi's midrash: when the advocate (Abraham) fell silent, the judge (the LORD) went away. The English gives the plain sense of the departure after the speech; the allegory is recorded here.

Rashi, again allegorically: once the judge and then the advocate had gone, the accuser remained and the two angels went to Sodom to destroy it. The English keeps the plain 'returned to his place'; the allegory is recorded here.

Ibn Ezra identifies 'his place' as Hebron: the vision took place where Abraham had gone to send the angels, from where he looked over Sodom; the sun had risen when he looked, since Sodom was not overturned at night. The English says 'his place' and does not name Hebron; the identification is recorded here.

apparatus: Onkelos renders the subject as 'the Glory of the LORD' (yeqara d'Adonai); the English keeps 'the LORD', the Hebrew word.

Radak (not normative) reads the departure as the end of the prophetic vision: Abraham found himself back in his house where he had been sitting. Sforno: Abraham waited there until the Shekhinah withdrew. Neither is adopted.

segments.english: The two angels came to Sodom in the evening, and Lot was sitting in the gate of Sodom. When Lot saw them, he rose to meet them and bowed down, nose to the ground.
segments.literal: and-came two the-angels to-Sodom in-the-evening and-Lot sitting in-gate-of Sodom and-saw Lot and-rose to-meet-them and-bowed-down nostrils to-the-ground

tokens.note: wayyiqtol of bo'. The arrival is in Sodom; the sense is 'come'.
malakh sent by God; the decisions give 'angel'. See the commentary on 19:1 for the name.
directional he on Sodom.
beth with the article: 'in the evening'.
qal active participle, masculine singular: a background description, 'was sitting'.
construct state: 'the gate of'.
wayyiqtol of ra'ah. The Hebrew gives no object; the English supplies 'them'.
wayyiqtol of qum, 'arise'.
lamed with the infinitive construct of qara', 'meet' (homograph of qara', 'call'); the suffix 'them' is in this token.
wayyiqtol hitpael of shaḥah: prostrate oneself.
Dual of אַף: the two nostrils. 'Nose to the ground' is the plain picture of a full prostration; BDB also lists 'face' (2) for this idiom.
directional he on erets.

phrases.english: The two angels came to Sodom in the evening
phrases.literal: 'and-came two the-angels to-Sodom in-the-evening': the verb comes first, the subject follows.

phrases.english: and Lot was sitting in the gate of Sodom
phrases.literal: 'and-Lot sitting in-gate-of Sodom': a participle gives the background to the next action.
'and-saw Lot': the object of the seeing is not written; 'them' is supplied from the context.
'and-rose to-meet-them': the sequence of the two verbs.

phrases.english: and bowed down, nose to the ground
phrases.literal: 'and-bowed-down nostrils to-the-ground': the dual אַפַּיִם is the two nostrils (Ibn Ezra); the English 'nose'.

grammar: The chain of wayyiqtols (came, saw, rose, bowed down) gives the narrative sequence: the arrival, the sighting, the rising and the bowing.
The dual shenei (two) with the definite noun 'the angels' is a construct phrase: 'two of the angels' is read as 'the two angels'.
yoshev (19:1.7) is a participle: the English 'was sitting' gives the state that Lot is in when the angels arrive.
The dual apayim (19:1.15), 'nostrils', is the adverbial accusative of the bowing: 'bowed down, nostrils to the ground'; the hitpael of shaḥah means 'prostrate oneself'.
segments.note: The English 'he rose to meet them' keeps the subject Lot; the verb 'rose' with the lamed infinitive is a sequence of two actions.

commentary.summary: Rashi (after the Talmud and Bereshit Rabbah): of the three visitors of 18:2, one went to destroy Sodom, one to save Lot (the same who had come to heal Abraham), and the third, who came to tell Sarah, left once his task was done. A midrash on the errands; the English 'two' is the text's own number.

Rashi: with Abraham they are called 'men' because the Shekhinah was with them; another explanation: Abraham's strength was great and the angels were constantly with him like men, but with Lot (who is lesser) they are called 'angels' (Bereshit Rabbah). The English 'angels' is the plain word; Rashi's reasons for the change of term are recorded.

Rashi asks whether the angels really took so long from Hebron to Sodom, and answers that they were angels of mercy who waited in case Abraham could find a defence for the city. A homily on the delay; 'in the evening' keeps the plain time.
Rashi: 'and Lot was sitting' is written with yashav; that day they made him judge over them (Bereshit Rabbah). The English 'was sitting' keeps the plain sense; the judgeship reading is recorded here.
Rashi: Lot learned from Abraham's house to go out and meet guests. A comment on conduct; the English reports the act.

Ibn Ezra's whole comment is 'and its explanation, בערב: at the Passover of Egypt' (בפסח מצרים), a cross-reference to his treatment of 'evening' in connection with the Passover in Egypt. It adds nothing to the sense of the verse; the English 'in the evening' stands.
Ibn Ezra: אַפַּיִם is 'until he put his nostrils on the earth': they are the nostrils, which are high on the face. Lot bowed with his nose to the ground. The English now follows this.

apparatus: Targum Onkelos renders the bowing as 'on his face (al apohi) on the ground'; Ibn Ezra takes the dual as the nostrils, and the English follows him. 'Face' (BDB 2) is the other sense.
context: The city gate was the public space of an ancient town: a roofed or chambered passage where people met, did business and sat in judgment. A man sitting in the gate is a townsman in the public place.
Bowing to the ground was the formal greeting to a superior or an honoured guest; it expresses courtesy and respect and is not an act of worship.

segments.english: And he said, "Here now, my lords, turn aside, please, to your servant's house and spend the night, and wash your feet; then you can rise early and go on your way." But they said, "No, but we will spend the night in the square."
segments.literal: and-said Here now my-lords turn-aside please to house-of your-servant and-spend-the-night and-wash your-feet and-rise-early and-go to-your-way and-said no for in-the-square we-spend-the-night

tokens.note: hinneh, an exclamation: 'here' or 'look'; never 'behold' in English.
na, interjection, 'now', 'please' (see 19:2.6).
adonai with pataḥ: 'my lords' (decisions: 19:2 is the plural of address to the men).
imperative plural of sur, 'turn aside'.
na, exhortation, 'please'.
construct state: 'the house of'.
construct with the 2mp suffix; 'your servant' is Lot's address to the men.
imperative of lun, 'pass the night'.
imperative of rahats.
dual construct with the 2mp suffix.
qatal with vav, continuing the imperatives: 'then you can rise early'.
qatal with vav (weqatal) of הָלַךְ, 'go': it continues the imperatives as a consequence ('and go'). BDB Qal I.1, of persons.
lamed with the construct of derekh and the 2mp suffix.
wayyiqtol of amar; the vav is adversative here.
lo, the negative particle.
ki, read as 'but' (ela) by Rashi; see the commentary.
beth with the article on rehov, 'broad open place'.
yiqtol first person common plural of lun.

phrases.literal: 'and-said': the vav opens the speech.
'Here now my-lords': the exclamation with the address.
'turn-aside please': the imperative with the particle of entreaty.
'to house-of your-servant': the construct chain, with Lot's address to the men.

phrases.english: and spend the night, and wash your feet
phrases.literal: 'and-spend-the-night and-wash your-feet': the Hebrew order (lodge first, then wash) is kept.

phrases.english: then you can rise early and go on your way
phrases.literal: 'and-rise-early and-go to-your-way': the qatal forms continue the imperatives as a consequence.
'and-said': the men's reply, adversative.

phrases.english: No, but we will spend the night in the square
phrases.literal: 'no for in-the-square we-spend-the-night': the refusal, then the alternative.

grammar: The imperatives suru, vilinu and verahatsu (plural) address the men; the vav links the imperatives in a request.
Hinneh na is an exclamation with the particle na: 'here now'. The second na (19:2.6) is an exhortation, 'please'.
The qatal forms vehishkamtem and vahalakhtem (19:2.13-14) continue the imperatives: 'then you can rise early and go on your way'.
lo ... ki (19:2.17-18) is 'No, but': ki is adversative here, as Rashi reads it.
segments.note: The imperative 'spend the night' (lun) and the yiqtol 'we will spend the night' (19:2.20) use the same verb: the men refuse Lot's offer of a night in his house.

commentary.summary: Rashi: 'here now, my lords' means you are my lords now that you have passed through me; his second reading, that the men must take care not to be recognised by the wicked men of the city, is recorded here. The English 'my lords' follows the address.

Rashi: 'turn aside' means make the road to my house crooked, so that Sodom does not see them going in (Bereshit Rabbah). The English keeps the plain 'turn aside'; the crooked-road reading is recorded.

Rashi explains the order 'spend the night, then wash': Lot wanted their feet to show the dust of the road, so that Sodom would not say they had been in his house for days. The English keeps the Hebrew order; the motive is recorded here.
Rashi: they refused Lot, a lesser man, but did not refuse Abraham (18:5). A comment on the refusal; the English 'No' stands.
Rashi: ki here means 'but' (ela): they would not turn aside to his house but would spend the night in the city square. The English 'No, but' follows.

Ibn Ezra: 'my lords' (רבותי) is secular speech, a courtesy to men and not the Name. He adds that when סור is followed by מ it means 'depart from'; when it is followed by אל with a short pataḥ (אֶל) it means that the person leaves his place and goes to the one who calls or to the place named, as in 'Turn aside to me' (Judg. 4:18). So סורו נא אל בית עבדכם is 'turn aside to your servant's house'.

Ibn Ezra glosses the refusal לא as 'if you do not press' (אם לא תפצר): a courteous 'no' that waits to be pressed. He adds that the verb 'press' (הפצר, as in 1 Sam. 15:23 'ואון ותרפים הפצר') means a multitude of words, in the sense of entreaties. The English 'No' is the plain negative; his conditional reading is recorded, and it explains why Lot presses them in 19:3.

apparatus: WLC note v on 19:2.14 (vahalakhtem): one or more vowels in the Leningrad codex are read differently from BHS. The pointing in the pack is followed.
context: Washing the feet of a guest was an ordinary act of hospitality in a land of dusty roads and open sandals (see 18:4).

A traveller who reached a town at nightfall without a host could spend the night in the open square inside the town; a parallel scene is Judges 19:15-21. Taking a stranger into one's house put him under the host's protection.

segments.english: But he urged them strongly, and they turned aside to him and came into his house. He made a feast for them and baked unleavened bread, and they ate.
segments.literal: and-urged in-them greatly and-turned-aside to-him and-came to-house-of-him and-made for-them feast and-unleavened-cakes baked and-ate

tokens.note: wayyiqtol of patsar, 'press, urge'. The vav is adversative here.
beth with the 3mp suffix: 'upon them'.
me'od, 'exceedingly, greatly'.
wayyiqtol of sur, 'turn aside' (see 19:2.5).
wayyiqtol of bo', 'come in'.
wayyiqtol of asah, 'make'.
lamed with the 3mp suffix.
mishteh, from shathah, 'drink'; a meal, not a sense in the lexicon.
vav with matsah, feminine plural.
qatal of afah, 'bake'.
wayyiqtol of akhal, 'eat'. The subject is the two men.

phrases.literal: 'and-urged in-them greatly': the adversative vav; the object 'them' comes after the verb in the English.

phrases.english: and they turned aside to him and came into his house
phrases.literal: 'and-turned-aside to-him and-came to-house-of-him': the men yield and come in.

phrases.english: He made a feast for them
phrases.literal: 'and-made for-them feast': the verb and the object.
'and-unleavened-cakes baked': the English puts the verb before the object.
'and-ate': the closing wayyiqtol.

grammar: The wayyiqtols (urged, turned aside, came, made, ate) carry the narrative. The vav of 'urged' is adversative: the men had refused, and Lot presses them.
The adverb me'od (19:3.3) intensifies the verb: 'greatly'. The preposition beth on the 3mp suffix gives the object of the urging.
The meal is named by two nouns, mishteh and matsot, and one verb, afah: the Hebrew names the feast before the baking. The English reverses the order.
segments.note: The verb 'turned aside' (vayyasuru) is the same as 19:2.5 'turn aside'. The men who refused the road now turn to Lot's house.

commentary.summary: Rashi: 'they turned aside to him' means they bent the road toward his house (as in his comment at 19:2, that Lot bent the road so as not to be seen). The English 'turned aside to him' is the plain departure from the road; Rashi's crooked-road sense is recorded.
Rashi: the unleavened bread shows that it was Passover. The English keeps 'unleavened bread' and does not name the feast; the Passover reading is recorded here.
Ramban (not normative): Lot had merit in pressing the men, and they were reluctant at first. A comment on Lot's character; not the plain sense of the words.

Radak (not normative): if the event was in a vision, it is as it reads; if Lot was awake and felt it, it seemed to him they ate and drank, since the food and drink, being compounds, returned to their simple first elements, each to its origin, as a miracle. The English keeps 'they ate'; the reading is recorded.

apparatus: Targum Onkelos (19:3) renders the urging as 'and he pressed them'; the English keeps 'urged' with the adverb 'strongly'.
context: Unleavened bread is flat bread baked at once, without waiting for the dough to rise; it was what a host could prepare in a short time for guests who arrived late (see 18:6 for the same hurry). The text does not tie it to a festival; Rashi reads it as Passover.

segments.english: Before they lay down, the men of the city, the men of Sodom, surrounded the house, from boys to old men, all the people, from the far edge of the city.
segments.literal: before they-lay-down the-men-of the-city the-men-of Sodom surrounded upon the-house from-youth and-to old all the-people from-end

tokens.note: teram, 'before, not yet'; it takes a yiqtol.
yiqtol of shakhav, 'lie down' (to sleep).
vav not rendered in the English.
construct, in apposition to 'the men of the city'.
nifal qatal of sabav, 'turn oneself, close round'.
al: absorbed in 'surrounded' in the English.
mi with na'ar: 'from youth'.
vav with ad, 'to, until'.
adjective used as a noun: 'old man'; the pair נַעַר-זָקֵן names the whole age range.
kol in construct with ha'am, 'the whole of'.
מִ + קָצֶה, 'from the end, the edge'. The city is understood. Ibn Ezra: people came who were not near the house; Rashi: from one end of the city to the other.

phrases.literal: 'before they-lay-down': the temporal particle with the yiqtol.

phrases.english: the men of the city, the men of Sodom
phrases.literal: 'the-men-of the-city the-men-of Sodom': the second phrase names the first, the wicked men.
'surrounded upon the-house': the preposition is absorbed in the English verb.
'from-boy and-to old': the range from the youngest to the oldest.
'all the-people'.

phrases.english: from the far edge of the city
phrases.literal: 'from-end': from the edge, that is, from far from the house (Ibn Ezra); Rashi: from one end of the city to the other.

grammar: Teram with the yiqtol (before they lay down) is a temporal clause. The English uses the past, since the narrative is past.
The phrase 'the men of the city, the men of Sodom' is an apposition: the men of the city are the men of Sodom, the wicked.
nasabu is nifal (Niph) qatal, 'they surrounded'. The stem gives a middle sense, 'close round the house'.
segments.note: The verse is a single long sentence: the time clause, the subject and the verb, then the range of ages and the closing phrase.

commentary.summary: Rashi gives the midrash first (the angels asked Lot about the men and he said most of them were wicked), then the plain sense: the men of the city were wicked and are called men of Sodom, as in 13:13. The English follows the plain sense; the midrashic setting is not adopted.

Rashi: מִקָּצֶה is 'from the end of the city to the end', so that not one of them protested and not even one righteous man was among them. The English 'from the far edge of the city' keeps the spatial sense; Rashi's 'one end to the other' and the point about the righteous are recorded.
Ibn Ezra: the verb is nifal. The English 'surrounded' follows the stem, a middle sense of 'close round'.
Ibn Ezra: 'all the people from the end' means that they were not near the house. The English now says that the crowd came even from the far edge of the city.

apparatus: Targum Onkelos on 19:4 has 'from young to old' (me'ulimah ve'ad saba), with 'surrounded the house'; the English follows the Hebrew.

segments.english: And they called to Lot and said to him, "Where are the men who came to you tonight? Bring them out to us, that we may lie with them."
segments.literal: and-called to Lot and-said to-him where the-men who-came to-you the-night bring-them-out to-us and-that-we-know them

tokens.note: wayyiqtol of qara' with el, 'call to'. Homograph: qara' 'meet' (s.cz.aa) is different.
lamed with the 3ms suffix.
ayyeh, interrogative: 'where'.
ha-anashim: 'the men'.
asher, the relative particle.
qatal of bo', 'come'.
el with the 2ms suffix.
ha-laylah, 'the night': the English 'tonight'.
hifil imperative of yatsa' with the 3mp suffix.
el with the 1cp suffix.

tokens.gloss: and that we may lie with
tokens.note: cohortative of yada', 'know'. Here a euphemism for intercourse: Rashi and Ibn Ezra both take it so (see commentary).
the direct object marker with the 3mp suffix; no separate English word.

phrases.literal: 'and-called to Lot': the verb with el means 'call to'.
'and-said to-him'.

phrases.english: Where are the men who came to you tonight
phrases.literal: 'where the-men who-came to-you the-night': the question; 'are' is supplied in the English.
'bring-them-out to-us': the imperative.

phrases.english: that we may lie with them
phrases.literal: 'and-that-we-know them': the vav of purpose and the cohortative, with the euphemism.

grammar: The imperative hotsi (19:5.12) carries the 3mp suffix 'them'; the English gives 'bring them out to us'.

The cohortative venedaah (19:5.14) is 'let us know' with the vav of purpose: 'that we may know'. Ibn Ezra calls the verb a euphemism for lying (כנוי לשכיבה); BDB Qal 3, 'know a person'. The English 'lie with' keeps the euphemism.
The construction qara' el (19:5.1) means 'call to'. The homograph qara' 'meet' is not used here.
segments.note: The speech is direct: the men speak to Lot and the English puts it in double quotes. 'Know' is the verb of 19:5.14; the English is the commentators' reading of it.

commentary.summary: Rashi: 'that we may know them' means lying with a male, as in 'who had not known a man' (Bereshit Rabbah). The English 'that we may lie with them' follows.
Ibn Ezra: ונדעה אותם is a euphemism (כנוי) for lying down (שכיבה): the men of Sodom ask for sexual use of the visitors. The English 'lie with' keeps the euphemism.

Radak (not normative): 'who are they, and how did they not fear to come to our city, being strangers?' - that is, they said it to kill them, as ונדעה in the concubine at Gibeah (Judg. 19:22), where the man says 'they meant to kill me' (Judg. 20:5). Some explain it as lying with a male. The English takes Rashi's and Ibn Ezra's sexual sense; Radak's 'kill' is recorded.

apparatus: Ramban (not normative) says the men's aim was to put an end to the traffic of strangers, as in Sanhedrin 109: they feared that the land's goodness would draw many to it, and they despised charity (Ezek. 16:49). The English follows Ibn Ezra's euphemism for lying.
context: The demand is for sexual abuse of strangers, which breaks the duty of hospitality; Judges 19:22-25 tells a parallel scene. The verb 'know' with a person as object is the usual Hebrew euphemism for sexual relations, but some commentators (Radak) read it here as 'to question' or 'to do them harm'.

segments.english: Lot went out to them, to the doorway, and shut the door behind him.
segments.literal: and-went-out to-them Lot to-the-doorway and-the-door shut behind-him

tokens.note: wayyiqtol of yatsa'.
directional he on petah, 'opening, doorway'.
vav with the article and delet.
qatal of sagar, 'shut'.
achar with the 3ms suffix.

phrases.literal: 'and-went-out to-them Lot': the verb and then the subject.
'to-the-doorway': the directional he, 'to the opening' (Ibn Ezra: אל הפתח).

phrases.english: and shut the door behind him
phrases.literal: 'and-the-door shut behind-him': the object comes first in the Hebrew; the English puts the verb before it.

grammar: The wayyiqtol 'went out' is followed by the qatal 'shut' in a second clause: the narrative continues with the act of closing.
The directional he on petah (19:6.4) gives the place towards which Lot goes: the doorway.
The preposition achar with the 3ms suffix gives 'behind him'.
segments.note: The subject of the shutting is Lot in the English; Radak allows the man inside to have shut it.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra glosses הַפֶּתְחָה as אל הפתח, 'to the opening', the final he being directional; he adds that the tav of דלת is the sign of the feminine and that the noun is 'found lacking'. A grammatical note; the English 'to the doorway' is the sense he gives.
Radak (not normative): 'shut' may mean that the man inside shut the door, or that Lot shut it from outside. The English gives Lot's act; Radak's alternative is recorded.

segments.english: And he said, "Please, my brothers, do not act wickedly."

tokens.note: al with the yiqtol: a prohibition.
na, 'please'.
construct plural with the 1cs suffix: 'my brothers'; addressed to the men of the city.
yiqtol hifil of ra'a, 'do evil, wickedly'.

phrases.literal: 'and-said': the speech.

phrases.english: Please, my brothers, do not act wickedly
phrases.literal: 'do-not please my-brothers act-wickedly': the prohibition, with the English word order.

grammar: al with the yiqtol (19:7.2 and 19:7.5) is a prohibition: 'do not act wickedly'.
The particle na (19:7.3) softens the prohibition to a request: 'please'.
The hifil of ra'a (19:7.5) carries the sense 'do evil': the English 'act wickedly' takes the second sense listed.
segments.note: Lot's speech is a plea, not a command: the English 'please' keeps the particle na.

commentary.summary: Radak (not normative): 'please' is a request that the men do not harm these people. The English 'please' and the prohibition follow his reading.

Radak: 'my brothers' means 'my neighbours', and the request is that they leave these men for the sake of his honour. The English keeps 'my brothers', the Hebrew word; the neighbour reading is recorded here.
Targum Onkelos renders 'do not act wickedly' as la tav'ishun, 'do not do evil, do not harm'. This is the same sense as the English; it does not mean 'shame'.
